h1: Invoice from the driveway. Get paid before you leave.
subtitle: Plumbers and HVAC techs lose hours every week to evening paperwork. Invoicor lets you build a complete invoice from your phone while still on-site, separate dispatch fees from parts and labor cleanly, and let the homeowner tap-to-pay with Apple Pay before you pull out of the driveway.
industry_mistakes_title: Billing mistakes that cost plumbers and HVAC techs money
industry_mistake_1_text: When you roll the diagnostic or callout fee into the labor line, homeowners see an inflated hourly rate and push back. Listing dispatch as its own line item makes the cost of you driving to the property visible and defensible.
industry_mistake_2_title: Not breaking out parts and labor.
industry_mistake_2_text: Most US states tax materials but not labor (or tax them at different rates). One blended line item creates tax-filing headaches at year-end and often results in overpaying sales tax. Always split parts and labor into distinct rows with the correct tax flag on each.
industry_mistake_3_text: Emergency Saturday calls justify a premium rate, but only if it's documented on the invoice. Techs who quote a flat rate verbally and forget to apply the after-hours multiplier on the written invoice lose money on every weekend job.
feature_1_text: Save your standard dispatch fee, weekend multiplier, and emergency rate as reusable line items in your product library. Adding them to an invoice takes one tap, so you never forget to apply them on a Saturday job.
feature_2_title: Separate parts and labor with tax flags
feature_2_text: Tag materials lines as taxable and labor lines as non-taxable (or vice versa, depending on your state). Invoicor calculates the correct sales tax automatically and your year-end export is already clean for your accountant.
feature_3_text: Text or email the invoice link directly to the homeowner. They open it on their phone, tap Apple Pay or Google Pay, and the payment clears before you've packed up your tools. No more waiting on mailed checks.
expert_tip_title: Pro Tip: Always list dispatch as a separate line item
expert_tip_text: List your diagnostic or dispatch fee on its own row, distinct from the actual repair labor. This reduces sticker shock for the homeowner, justifies the cost of driving to their property, and gives you a clean upgrade path if you ever want to waive dispatch as a sales incentive on larger repair jobs.
real_scenario_text: 8:14 AM Saturday call: homeowner has a leaking water heater. You arrive at 8:45, diagnose a failed T&P relief valve in 15 minutes, drive to the supply house, return with the replacement part, complete the install and pressure test by 11:30. From the kitchen counter, you build the invoice in Invoicor: $95 emergency callout fee (weekend rate, non-taxable labor), $42 T&P relief valve (taxable parts), $180 install labor (1.5 hours at $120/hr, non-taxable). Total: $317 plus calculated sales tax on the part only. You text the link to the homeowner, she pays via Apple Pay while you're loading the van. You're home for lunch by noon, paid in full.

industry_glossary_title: Plumbing and HVAC billing terms explained

industry_glossary.definition: A flat fee charged for the technician arriving on-site, separate from the cost of any work performed. Justifies vehicle, fuel, and travel time. Typically $75-$150 standard, $150-$300 emergency.
A billing method where the customer pays the actual labor hours plus the cost of materials, rather than a single flat-rate quote. Common for diagnostic or open-ended repair work.
A fixed price for a defined service (e.g. 'water heater flush: $189') regardless of actual time spent. Protects the tech if a job runs long and gives the customer price certainty.
The plumbing work installed before walls are closed up on a new build or renovation. Usually invoiced as a milestone payment, not a flat rate.
Temperature and pressure relief valve on a water heater. A common high-frequency replacement part on emergency callouts.

tax_or_compliance_title: Sales tax on plumbing and HVAC invoices
tax_or_compliance_text: In most US states, materials used in plumbing and HVAC work are subject to sales tax, while labor is not. A handful of states (notably Hawaii, New Mexico, South Dakota, West Virginia) tax both. The cleanest approach: tag every line item on your invoice as either 'parts' (taxable) or 'labor' (non-taxable) at the time you create the invoice, so the tax calculation is correct by default. Invoicor's per-line tax flags handle this automatically and your year-end CSV export already has the categorization your accountant needs. Check your specific state's department of revenue for the exact rules; this is a common source of audit issues for trade businesses.

faqs.question: Can I separate parts and labor on the invoice with different tax rates?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every line item has its own tax flag, so you can mark materials (PVC, copper pipe, HVAC units, refrigerant) as taxable and labor lines as non-taxable, exactly matching your state's rules. The tax total at the bottom of the invoice only applies to the lines you marked as taxable.

faqs.question: How do I handle large deposits for HVAC installs?
faqs.answer: For high-ticket jobs like a full furnace or AC unit installation, create an invoice for the total amount and send a partial-payment request for the deposit (commonly 50%). The customer pays the deposit via card to lock in the install date. After completion, you send a second invoice for the balance, or convert the original to mark the deposit as received and bill the remaining amount.

faqs.question: Can homeowners pay without downloading an app?
faqs.answer: Yes. The payment link goes to a secure web portal that opens in any phone or laptop browser. The homeowner taps the link, sees the full invoice, and pays with their credit card, Apple Pay, or Google Pay. No account creation, no app install, no friction. This matters for older homeowners who won't download a billing app.

faqs.question: What if I need to invoice a commercial property manager instead of a homeowner?
faqs.answer: Same flow, but you can save the property management company as a client with their billing email and net-30 payment terms baked in. Many commercial property managers prefer email-based ACH bank transfer rather than card payments to avoid processing fees on larger invoices; Invoicor's payment link supports both.

faqs.question: Does Invoicor handle multi-truck or multi-tech operations?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you run multiple trucks under the same business, all your techs can send invoices that flow into the same business profile, so your accounts receivable view shows every open invoice across the operation. If you run completely separate businesses (e.g. plumbing LLC and HVAC LLC under different EINs), use multi-business profile switching to keep them isolated with their own logos, tax setups, and client lists.

industry_mistakes_title: Billing mistakes that cost freelance designers money
industry_mistake_1_title: Starting work before the deposit clears.
industry_mistake_1_text: The number one reason freelance designers don't get paid is that they start delivering value before the deposit is in the bank. A signed contract is not a payment. Always send the deposit invoice the moment the contract is signed, and don't open Figma until the money clears.
industry_mistake_2_title: Not capping revision rounds in writing.
industry_mistake_2_text: 'Just one more revision' is the design industry's most expensive sentence. Specify on every invoice (and contract) exactly how many revision rounds are included in the project scope, and what the hourly rate is for additional rounds. When you have it documented, scope creep becomes additional billable work instead of an awkward conversation.
industry_mistake_3_text: When a European client pays a USD invoice, they absorb the FX conversion cost on their end, which often inflates your invoice by 3-5% in their eyes. Sending the invoice in their local currency (EUR, GBP, AUD) makes you look more professional and removes a hesitation point. The conversion happens automatically when they pay, and the funds land in your account in your currency.
feature_1_text: Upload your high-resolution logo (PNG with transparency for that crisp look), set your exact brand hex colors, and pick from 30 designed templates ranging from minimal Swiss-style to premium textured layouts. feature_2_text: Send a 50% deposit invoice the moment the contract is signed. When the deposit clears, the milestone updates automatically. On final delivery, generate the balance invoice with one tap; the line items remember what was already paid, so your numbers always reconcile.
feature_3_text: Bill a London agency in GBP, a Berlin startup in EUR, a Sydney brand in AUD. Your client pays in their local currency via card or bank transfer; the funds land in your account in your home currency, with the FX conversion handled by Stripe. No more awkward 'just send dollars please' emails.
expert_tip_title: Pro Tip: Always invoice the deposit before any deliverable goes out
expert_tip_text: Set a personal rule: no mood board, no wireframe, no Figma file leaves your machine until the deposit has cleared. Not 'signed contract', not 'deposit invoice sent' — cleared. This is the single highest-leverage habit a freelance designer can build. Clients who push back on this rule are also the clients most likely to ghost on the balance payment later. Use the deposit clearance as a filter, not just a payment milestone.

real_scenario_text: $8,000 brand identity project, four-week timeline. Contract signed Monday. industry_glossary.definition: An upfront payment (typically 50% of total project value) collected before any work begins. Protects the designer if the client cancels or ghosts mid-project. Industry standard for any project over $1,000.

A pre-agreed payment owed to the designer if the client terminates the project before completion. Usually 25-50% of the remaining balance. Specified in the contract and surfaced on the invoice as a line-item placeholder.

What the client is allowed to do with the final design files (commercial use, geographic scope, time limit, exclusivity). Often a separate line item on the invoice, with rights transferring only on final payment.

tax_or_compliance_title: VAT and tax for designers billing internationally
tax_or_compliance_text: Designers in the EU billing other EU businesses typically use the reverse-charge mechanism: your invoice excludes VAT but includes both VAT numbers and a note like 'VAT reverse-charged per Article 196 of the EU VAT Directive'. Designers in the US billing US clients generally don't charge sales tax on design services (most states classify them as non-taxable services), but a handful of states (notably Hawaii, New Mexico, South Dakota, West Virginia) do tax services — check your state's rules. UK designers post-Brexit charge VAT on UK clients only and zero-rate exports; the invoice must show your VAT number and the client's country to be compliant. Invoicor lets you save these tax configurations per business profile, so once you set it up correctly, every future invoice handles it automatically.

faqs.question: Can I attach my design contract or SOW to the invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can attach PDFs of your Master Services Agreement, Statement of Work, or signed contract directly to the invoice email. Larger clients with formal PO systems often require the SOW number printed on the invoice itself; you can add this as a custom field that appears at the top of the document.

faqs.question: How do I charge international clients without losing money on FX?
faqs.answer: Invoicor supports over 135 currencies. Send the invoice in your client's local currency (EUR, GBP, AUD, etc.) and they pay via card or bank transfer in that currency. Stripe handles the FX conversion at near-interbank rates, and funds deposit into your bank in your home currency. You lose far less to FX than if you invoiced in USD and made the client absorb their bank's conversion fee.

faqs.question: Can I send a deposit invoice and a balance invoice for the same project?
faqs.answer: Yes. The standard freelance pattern is two invoices per project: invoice A for the 50% deposit (sent at contract signing, payable before kickoff), and invoice B for the balance (sent on final delivery). Both invoices can reference the same project name or SOW number, so your client's accounting system links them automatically. Some designers also do thirds: deposit, milestone, delivery.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to pay via wire transfer instead of card?
faqs.answer: Larger agencies and corporate clients often prefer ACH or international wire over card, because the processing fees on a $10,000 card transaction can be $300+. Invoicor invoices include your bank details (configurable per business profile) as an alternative payment method. The client picks whichever they prefer; you get paid either way.

faqs.question: How do I handle revision-round overages without ruining the client relationship?
faqs.answer: The trick is to surface revision rounds on the original invoice as a clearly-scoped line item: 'Includes 2 revision rounds'. When the client asks for round 3, you reference the original invoice and add 'Additional Revision Round' as a new line at your hourly rate. It's now a documented scope decision rather than a surprise charge, and most clients accept it without friction because they agreed to the limit upfront.
